title: How the Fairness Doctrine Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck open with live tour dates and banter about cursing on the show, then explain the Fairness Doctrine: its origins in early radio and spectrum scarcity, the Radio Act of 1912 and Titanic, the Radio Act of 1927 and Federal Communications Act of 1934, the 1941 Mayflower decision, the fairness rule components (personal attack and political editorial rules), the cigarette advertising ruling, key court cases (Red Lion, United Church of Christ v. FCC over WLBT), the 1987-era repeal process, Reagan's veto of codification, and its legacy and polarization debate. Ends with listener mail about voice colors and perfect pitch.
topics: United Church of Christ v. FCC

segments.title: Tour dates and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck promote upcoming live shows in Chicago, Toronto, Boston, Portland Maine, Orlando, New Orleans and Brooklyn, then joke about cursing on the show.

segments.title: Early radio and KDKA's 1920 election broadcast
segments.summary: The hosts describe the sparse early radio era dominated by ham operators, then KDKA in Pittsburgh broadcasting the Harding-Cox election results in November 1920, and the rapid spread of radios in the 1920s.

segments.title: What the Fairness Doctrine is
segments.summary: Overview of the Fairness Doctrine's goal of ensuring good information over broadcaster free speech, tied to spectrum scarcity, and its core components: the fairness rule, personal attack rule and political editorial rule, contrasted with the equal time rule.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A brief ad break before the history section.

segments.title: Origins: Titanic, Radio Act of 1912, and the Radio Act of 1927
segments.summary: Radio regulation begins after the Titanic disaster exposed congestion from ham operators; the Radio Act of 1912 required licenses; the Radio Act of 1927 created the Radio Commission and set the 'public interest, convenience or necessity' standard, which was vague.

segments.title: Federal Communications Act and the Mayflower decision
segments.summary: The Federal Communications Act replaced the Radio Act and created the FCC. The 1941 Mayflower decision barred broadcasters from editorializing, which the Fairness Doctrine later softened into a requirement to air both sides.

segments.title: Cigarette ads, case-by-case enforcement, and landmark court cases
segments.summary: The 1967 ruling treating cigarette advertising as a viewpoint, the case-by-case enforcement and resulting false balance problem, and the Red Lion case (Fred Cook and Reverend Billy James Hargis) and the WLBT license case, in which the Supreme Court upheld the doctrine and the FCC revoked WLBT's license.

segments.title: Decline, repeal, and legacy
segments.summary: Court shifts in the 1970s, the Harold Gross WJIM case, the 1980s growth of media outlets eroding spectrum scarcity argument, the FCC's move to abandon the rules, Reagan's veto of a codification bill, and the FCC's final removal in 2011. The hosts discuss polarization and the doctrine's legacy.

segments.title: Listener mail: voice colors
segments.summary: A listener from the Salt Lake City show describes hearing musical notes and voices as colors, with perfect pitch, and describes the hosts' voices.
